Present Perfect vs. Past Simple

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.
You use the Past Simple to talk an event in the past that is finished, which has no connection to the present.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.

Example:
Many professional athletes have become accustomed to hiding injuries.
= Athletes still get injuries in the present.
You use the Present Perfect Simple to talk about habitual actions or with state verbs, when there a connection to the present.

Example:
I've lived here for the past ten years.
= I still live here now.

You use the Past Simple to talk about an event in the past with no connection to the present or a present situation. When you use the Past Simple, the event in the past is finished, and it is usually an event that did not occur regularly or a habitual action.

Example:
I made my way down from my seat to the locker room.
= The situation only happens once and it is a finished action.

The Reason Clause

You use reason clauses to express the reasons for an action, or why a situation is the way it is.
You use words like because, since, as, in case, and seeing that to introduce a reason clause.

Reason clauses are subordinate to the main clause. They state the reason why things are done, or what makes a situation the way it is.
You can use the following words to introduce a reason clause:
• because
You use because to explain the reason why something is the way it is.
• since/as
You use since or as to introduce a reason that is already known.
• (just) in case
You use in case to talk about things that may possibly happen.
• seeing that
You use seeing that to state that a situation is known.

images.text:
Sports physician Steve Crayton has spent a lifetime perfecting the art of reading body language. He works exclusively with professional basketball players, and he has grown used to identifying injuries based on slight changes in a player's mannerisms.
“Many professional athletes have become accustomed to hiding injuries, since they don't want their opponents to find out and exploit their weakness,” says Dr. Crayton.

According to Dr. Crayton, players don't have to report injuries for him to become aware of them. “I can just watch the game,” he says. “If a player is slouching or grabbing his shorts, then he's winded. And if the player walks gingerly to the bench after a rough play, it's because he has a lower-body injury. He'll try to walk naturally, but it's obvious to me that he has sprained an ankle. Last week I was watching one of the guys play a game in Toronto,” he recalls. “I noticed him leaning slightly to the left of the foul line, because he was favoring his right ankle. Right away, I made my way down from my seat to the locker room, just in case his ankle needed to be bandaged.”

“Another telltale sign is a lack of concentration,” Dr. Crayton continues. “If a guy is looking out into the crowd and not following the play, I know he's received some kind of a head trauma. In those cases, I don't wait until halftime. I'll pull him right away, just in case it's a concussion.”
“It's a tricky job, it requires a great amount of attention to detail,” Dr. Crayton says, cracking a smile. “But I'm not complaining. After all, not many jobs allow you to sit courtside at a basketball game.”
